Question: Should schools place a heavy emphasis on grammar when teaching English as a second language? Or should more emphasis be put on real-life application for communicative purposes?
Answer: tl;dr: emphatically NO grammar. In countries which use the same (or very similar) alphabet, English should be taught in schools (assuming they start learning aged between 7 and 10) as follows: The purpose of this approach is to minimize resistance to English which is almost always caused by discussion of grammar, syntax and (especially) tenses if such discussions occur before the student is orally functional. Adult learners can easily compress this into 2 to 3 years part-time. Orally, English is very easy to learn because it is so prevalent and available worldwide. However, English spelling is idiotic, and we could actually do something about that, but we don’t because the same spellings are pronounced differently worldwide (and even within some quite small countries). English grammar is a topic of permanent debate. Tenses are nightmarishly difficult to analyse without first knowing how to use them. This is the worst error of English teaching historically: the idea that students can learn to use the tenses correctly if they are explained first. Doing this actively creates resistance because it makes many students think they will never be able to master it, because the explanation seems so counter-intuitive or confusing. What they don’t realize is that much of English grammar can only be explained badly. It’s neither the student nor the explanation that is at fault. The best way to avoid this resistance is to teach tense orally with NO EXPLANATION first. Once your students can manage both aspects in past, present and future, those who don’t get the grammatical analysis can safely ignore it. Which is what most native English speakers do. Seems to work okay for them.

Question: My school district is pressuring teachers to give students half credit (50%) instead of zeros for assignments not done. Is this happening in other school districts?
Answer: Something similar happens here in France, except it's marginally more ethical. At the end of a year, a panel of teachers considers the grades of each student, and may “choose” to adjust their grades to “better reflect” the student. You might think this would be a good way to mitigate problems like sickness, economic disadvantage and the other various accidents of life, until you learn that the overall goal is to ensure the school's average grade doesn't fall below a target set by the director. Both examples show how fucking stupid the idea of grading is.
